name: The Plaza 39
lead: Ten benches line the new square in front of a renovated office block, set on the paving's own grid so they read as part of the plan.
story: The square had been a car park for thirty years. The brief asked for seating that would last as long as the paving, with nothing to repaint. Galvanised frames and recycled boards meant the benches could go in on the same day as the trees, and the city's crews clean them with the rest of the square.

name: Sage Walk
lead: A row of park benches along a quiet residential walk, their sage frames chosen to sit with the hedges rather than against them.
story: Residents asked for places to stop on the way to the shops, every eighty metres or so. One model in one colour keeps the walk calm; the boards are recycled plastic, so the benches dry quickly after rain and never splinter.

name: Station Ring
lead: Recycling stations at the entrances of a regional rail station, each opening ringed in its stream's colour so travellers sort at a glance.
story: The station handles thirty thousand people a day, most of them in a hurry. Coloured rings around the openings do the explaining, without signs. The stations are bolted through the paving and emptied from the front in under a minute.

name: Harbour Steps
lead: Benches with armrests on the terraces above the harbour, where older visitors asked for something to push up from.
story: The terraces face west and catch the evening sun, so they fill up. Armrests on every bench were the residents' first request in the consultation. The frames are set back from the step edge so wheelchairs can pass in front.

name: Colour Courts
lead: Seven planters in seven colours mark the courtyards of a housing scheme, so children know which court is theirs.
story: The architect wanted each court to have its own colour without painting the buildings. Square planters in the shop palette carry it instead, and the planting is the same in all of them. Changing a colour later is a matter of one frame.

name: Sun Terrace
lead: Sun loungers on the terrace of a cultural centre, turned to the afternoon light and fixed so they stay where the plan put them.
story: The terrace was empty most of the year until the loungers arrived. Their warm white frames stay cool to the touch in summer, and the recycled boards are shaped to sit on as well as lie on.

name: Bike Yard
lead: Bike rack modules for a university faculty, their orange ends marking the rows from across the yard.
story: Bikes outnumber students at the faculty, so the racks had to take two hundred of them in a yard designed for half that. Modules join end to end, and the coloured supports show where a row stops and the path begins.

name: Depot Square
lead: A recycling station and a single-stream bin for each corner of a market square, in anthracite to match the lamp posts.
story: The market runs three days a week and leaves a lot behind. Stations sit at the corners where the stalls unload, smaller bins along the walk between them. All of them are emptied with the same key.

name: Long Quay
lead: Backless benches along a quay, so people can sit facing the water or the street, whichever has more going on.
story: A backless bench has no front: on a quay that is the point. They are spaced by the mooring rings, two metres long each, and low enough to step over without thinking about it.

name: Frame Colours
lead: The Frame bench with backrest in every colour of the palette, set out for a city's design review before it chose one.
story: The planning department wanted to see the colours outside, on real paving, not on a screen. The seven benches stayed for a month in front of the council offices. Petrol won, sage came second, and the others went to the city's schools.

name: Office Court
lead: Bike racks in the courtyard of an office building, where the orange supports double as a wayfinding mark from the entrance.
story: The courtyard had space for exactly four modules between the trees. The racks are bolted to the paving at both ends, and the galvanised tubes will look the same in twenty years.

name: Library Lawn
lead: Single-stream recycling bins on the lawn of a university library, in warm white so they read as part of the building's stone.
story: Students eat on the lawn from April to October. Bins were placed where the paths meet the grass, never on it, so the mowers can pass. The blue ring says paper, which is most of what the library throws away.

name: Low Line
lead: Backless benches along a new tram stop, low and long so people can wait without blocking the platform.
story: Tram stops need seats that do not take space. The backless bench sits at 46 cm, can be approached from both sides and leaves the platform edge free. The petrol frame is the colour of the shelters.

name: Garden Street
lead: Long and square planters turn a through road into a garden street, slowing traffic without a single sign.
story: The street was closed to through traffic in spring. Long planters narrow the carriageway, square ones mark the crossings, and the trees between them will take over in a few years. Everything can be lifted out with a forklift if the street changes again.

name: Weather Test
lead: Planters on a test site on the west coast of Norway, where we measure how the boards and the coating age in salt and rain.
story: Bergen has more rain than anywhere we deliver to. Three planters have stood on the test site for two years; the recycled boards have not moved, and the powder coat is checked against the colour card every six months.

name: Rail Racks
lead: Bike rack modules at a station's second entrance, laid out in two long rows that a cyclist can read from the road.
story: The station's main bike park was full by eight in the morning. Twenty-four modules took over a strip of grass at the back entrance. The rows run with the cycle path, so nobody has to turn against the flow to park.

name: Campus Edge
lead: Benches and planters at the edge of a campus, where the faculty buildings meet a public park.
story: The campus wanted to open towards the park without a fence. A line of backless benches with planters between them marks the edge instead, and gives the park a place to sit facing the buildings.

name: Picnic Meadow
lead: Picnic tables on the meadow of a city park, set on concrete pads so the grass around them survives the summer.
story: Families asked for tables, not benches: somewhere to put the food. The tables seat six and are fixed on pads at the meadow's edge, so the grass can be mowed right up to them.

name: Workshop Detail
lead: The board fixings of the Frame bench, photographed in our Venlo workshop for the installers' manual.
story: Every board is fixed from below with two stainless bolts, so nothing shows on the seat and nothing can be unscrewed from above. A single board can be replaced in ten minutes, without taking the bench off its base.

name: Mobility Hub
lead: Benches with an integrated bike stand at a mobility hub, where shared bikes, scooters and buses meet.
story: People waiting for a shared bike or a bus want to sit next to their own. The bench takes a bike against its end frame, so the hub needs no separate racks and stays open underfoot.

name: Station Bins
lead: Litter bins along the platforms of a city station, in the anthracite of the station's steelwork.
story: Twenty bins, one every forty metres, all emptied from the front with a single key. The slatted cladding hides the liner, and the hood keeps the rain out of it.

name: Gravel Park
lead: Backless benches on the gravel paths of a park, fixed on hidden foundations so the paths stay unbroken.
story: Most benches sink into gravel. These stand on small concrete foundations below the surface, so the gravel runs right up to the frame. The petrol frames echo the park's railings.

name: Sorting Colours
lead: Recycling stations in the full palette for a city that is choosing one colour per district.
story: Each district of the city will get its own colour of recycling station, so residents know which waste service runs where. The seven samples toured the districts for a month before each one voted.

name: Courtyard Five
lead: Benches with backrests in the fifth courtyard of a restored housing block, one under each tree.
story: The courtyards are small and shaded, used by the residents more than anyone else. A bench under each tree was all that was needed, with a backrest set for an hour's sitting.

name: Reuse Forecourt
lead: Wide benches made from reused boards on the forecourt of a recycling centre, which wanted its seating to say what it does.
story: The boards of the Reuse range are pressed again from our own offcuts. A recycling centre was the obvious first client. The wide seat works as a bench and as a table for people sorting their bags.

name: Rack Assembly
lead: The bike rack module taken apart: two side supports, galvanised tubes and the bolts, which is all an installer needs.
story: We designed the module so two people can install it without a crane. It arrives flat, goes together on site, and the side supports can be changed for another colour later without touching the tubes.

name: Canal Bench
lead: Backless benches on a canal bank, where the city asked for seats that do not block the view of the water.
story: Canal banks are narrow and protected. The backless bench keeps the view open from the houses, and its frame is anchored in the paving, not the quay wall, so the monument stays untouched.

name: Clinic Garden
lead: Benches with armrests in the garden of a clinic, for patients who need help to sit down and stand up again.
story: The clinic's physiotherapists checked the armrest height with us on a sample. The patients chose the sage from the palette, and the garden is now part of their daily walks.

name: Waste Corner
lead: A litter bin, a recycling bin and a recycling station grouped at the corners of a new residential street.
story: The street's waste points were designed in from the start, one every block. Three sizes cover what a household throws out on the way to work, and they share the same frame, so the corners look alike.

name: Market Hall
lead: Recycling stations at the doors of a covered market, with yellow and blue openings for packaging and paper.
story: Most of the market's waste is packaging. Two streams were enough, and the stations sit by the doors so people sort on their way out. The anthracite matches the hall's new steel roof.

name: Fixing Study
lead: The bike rack's fixings close up: each tube runs through the side support and is locked from inside.
story: Bike racks are pulled at, leaned on and driven into. The tubes pass through the supports and are locked from the inside, so there is no bolt head to unscrew and nothing to snag a wheel.

name: Reuse Terrace
lead: Reuse benches with backrests on the terrace of a riverside café, in warm white to suit the façade.
story: The café wanted benches that look at home with its tables and still belong to the street when it closes. The warm white frames and the reused boards do both.

name: Entrance Bins
lead: Litter bins at the entrance of an office campus, placed where people used to leave their rubbish on the paving.
story: Three bins solved what signs had not. They stand where people stop before going in, each one in sight of the next.

name: Roof Garden
lead: Square planters on the roof garden of a city library, deep enough for small trees and light enough for the roof.
story: Roof gardens are a question of weight. The planters' frames are steel, the cladding recycled plastic, and the liners take a light substrate, so twelve trees fit within the roof's load.

name: Rack Colours
lead: Bike racks in the full palette for a city's cycle parking review.
story: The city tests every new street object outside for a season. Seven racks, one per colour, stood on a busy corner; orange was the easiest to see at night, and became the standard for the new cycle routes.

name: Armrest Study
lead: The Plaza bench's armrest in accent orange, a special order for a children's playground.
story: The playground's designer wanted one colour that children would remember. The armrest is the part their hands find first, so that is where it went.

name: Byside Wall
lead: Backless benches along the blank wall of a sports hall, turning a dead side street into a place to wait.
story: The side street had nothing but a wall and a bus stop. Five benches along the wall made it somewhere to sit in the sun, and the planting strip behind them hides the drainage.

name: Lido Lawn
lead: Sun loungers on the lawn of an open-air lido, fixed in pairs so they stay out of the pool.
story: The lido's old loungers were plastic and ended up in the water every summer. The new ones are fixed in pairs on small foundations and turned to the afternoon sun.

name: Promenade
lead: Square planters along a promenade between shops and housing, each with a small tree and a ring of grasses.
story: The promenade was paved from wall to wall. Planters brought the trees in without breaking the paving or the cables below it, and they can be moved if the shops change.

name: Concert Square
lead: The Plaza bench with armrests on the square in front of a concert hall, galvanised so it needs nothing for decades.
story: The concert hall's square is the city's front room. Sixteen benches in two lengths face the hall's doors; galvanised steel and recycled boards mean no paint, no splinters and nothing to maintain.

name: Plaza Palette
lead: The Plaza bench with backrest in galvanised steel, seven of them set out for the city's street furniture catalogue.
story: The city keeps a catalogue of approved street furniture. The Plaza bench was photographed for it in a row of seven, as it will stand in most of the squares where it goes.

name: Wide Bench
lead: Reuse wide benches in a schoolyard, deep enough to sit on from either side or to lie on in the sun.
story: The school asked for benches that work for groups. The wide seat lets pupils sit back to back, face to face, or spread their lunch between them.

name: Bench Assembly
lead: The backless bench taken apart: two frames, a cross rail and the recycled boards, delivered flat and assembled on site.
story: Flat delivery means more benches on a truck and less fuel per bench. The frames are welded in our workshop; everything else is bolted on site with one tool.

name: Cycle Route
lead: Benches with bike stands along a long-distance cycle route, one at every rest point.
story: Cyclists on the route stop every twenty kilometres. Each rest point has a bench that holds a bike at its end, so riders can sit next to their bags.

name: Planter Court
lead: Square planters in the courtyard of an office building, where the trees are the only thing between the wall and the windows.
story: The courtyard gets little sun, so the planting is ferns and shade grasses. The planters raise them to sitting height, and their edges can be sat on.

name: Frame Group
lead: Frame benches with and without backrests, grouped around the trees of a new pocket park.
story: The park is small, so the benches are arranged in groups that face each other, three per tree. Backless ones for short stops, backrests for longer ones.

name: Recycled Boards
lead: The recycled plastic boards up close: pressed from household packaging, coloured through, with no coating to wear off.
story: The boards are brown all the way through, so a scratch is the same colour as the surface, and they can be pressed again at the end of their life.

name: Canteen Yard
lead: Picnic tables in the yard of a company canteen, so lunch can move outside whenever the weather allows.
story: The canteen seats two hundred inside and now sixty outside. The tables are fixed in a row along the façade, where the building shades them at midday.

name: Pocket Park
lead: Plaza benches set at angles under the trees of a pocket park, so every seat gets shade at some point of the day.
story: The park was a corner plot left over by a housing development. The benches are turned to follow the shade through the day, each one fixed on its own small foundation.

name: Backrest Study
lead: The backrest of the Reuse bench close up: boards fixed to a folded steel plate, with the bolts hidden from the seat.
story: The backrest's plate is folded from one sheet, which makes it stiff without a welded frame. The boards are fixed from behind, so the side people lean on is only plastic.

name: School Street
lead: Benches with backrests on a school street, closed to cars at the start and end of the school day.
story: Parents wait here twice a day. The benches face the school gate and are set back from the kerb, so the street still works for cars outside school hours.
